before.exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it shows in a sporting context. Simply reading a number earns nothing — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “Disabled students participate at 22% compared to 68% for male students — a gap of 46 percentage points — suggesting significant access or inclusion barriers for this group at this school.” On a 6 marks — Analyse question, avoid listing factors one by one. Instead, develop each point: name the factor, explain the mechanism, give a specific sporting example. A common error is addressing only one group. The spec requires knowledge of multiple social groups — aim to discuss at least two contrasting groups with specific barriers for each.

On 6-mark analyse questions about guidance, the most effective structure is: name the guidance type → explain its key feature → link it specifically to either a beginner or elite performer with a sporting example → justify why it suits that performer level. A common error is saying “visual guidance is good for beginners” without explaining why (beginners have no stored movement pattern to draw on, so seeing the skill demonstrated provides the mental blueprint they need). On the 6-mark evaluate question, always address both benefits and limitations of each guidance type, applying your points to the scenario. Read the scenario carefully — if the question specifies a beginner, the examiner wants to see why, for example, verbal guidance alone would be insufficient. Range of guidance types, balance (benefits and limitations) and consistent sporting application are what lift an answer into the top band.

On a “6-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sporting example. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progression” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: OCR names four principles — Specificity, Progression, Overload and Reversibility — and there is no Tedium principle. Confusing this with other boards’ acronyms is a common error.

On a “6-mark Evaluate” question about warm-up or cool-down, avoid simply listing components. The mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. For example, rather than writing “the pulse raiser raises heart rate,” develop it: “the pulse raiser gradually raises body temperature, which increases muscle pliability and reduces the risk of muscle strains — particularly important for a gymnast whose movements demand maximum hip and shoulder flexibility from the first routine.” For 2-mark “State Two” questions, ensure your two benefits are genuinely different physiological effects — “raises heart rate” and “increases blood flow” are related but distinct enough to earn two marks, whereas “raises heart rate” and “heart rate goes up” will only earn one. Note: OCR names five warm-up components, not four — mobility and dynamic movements are separate stages.

On a “6-mark Evaluate” question about injury prevention, the mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) balanced argument, and (c) sporting application. A common error is listing prevention strategies without explaining how they reduce injury — always link the strategy to the injury mechanism it prevents. For example: “Wearing shin pads in football reduces the risk of tibial fractures and lacerations from direct contact, because the pad absorbs and disperses the impact energy across a larger surface area.” For “Describe” questions about hazards, name the setting, name the specific hazard, and explain why it causes injury. Vague answers such as “the floor could be wet” without naming the setting or injury type will only earn one mark of a possible two or three. For that 6-mark question, weigh up which strategies are most effective and in which settings — PPE may be critical in contact sport but less relevant in swimming.
